source.filename: 2013-A Biologically Inspired Wet Shape Memory Alloy Actuated Robotic Pump.pdf

actuation: thermofluidic forced convection heating and cooling
constitutive_assumptions: Linear approximation of the fluid temperature gradient along the wire length assuming heat lost by the fluid equals heat entering the wire
Constant fluid flow velocity along the entire length of the SMA wire
SMA wire convective heat transfer governed by Newton's law of cooling
Hysteresis between martensite fraction and temperature approximated using a cumulative normal distribution curve
Piecewise linear elastic moduli for austenite, twinned martensite, and detwinned martensite regimes
Linear damping in the SMA wire strain rate equation
Fluidic resistance of check valves approaches infinity against reverse flow
Negligible heat loss to the environment and no mixing between hot and cold fluids in maximum theoretical efficiency calculations
control_variables: Joule heating electrical pulse duration (1.0 s)
Fluid stagnation period between flow cycles (2.0 s)
dependent_variables: Net volumetric fluid output flow rate (mL/min)
Temperature of fluid, tube, and SMA wire along the actuator length

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Wet SMA actuators envelop SMA wire inside compliant tubing to enable forced-convection thermofluidic heating and cooling for increased actuation rates with minimal spring resistance.

Theoretical feasibility constraints establish that achieving a net positive output-to-input ratio requires the ratio of fluidic area to wire area to satisfy specific bounds based on wire strain, actuation stress, accumulator pressure, and contraction-to-propagation time ratios.

The maximum theoretical thermodynamic efficiency of the wet SMA pumping system is calculated as 3.4% based on specific work output and transformation latent heat, assuming zero environmental heat loss and no fluid mixing.
Dynamic simulations based on energy bond graphs and discretized thermal convection predicted optimal pump output for actuator lengths between 35 cm and 45 cm and a mechanical advantage of 0.84.

Experimental output-to-input ratios for fluid-only actuation agreed within 5% to 10% of simulation predictions, reaching a maximum ratio of 0.88 without continuous accumulator heating under baseline operating conditions.

Combining continuous accumulator heating with supplementary electrical Joule heating (4.5 A for 1 s) enabled the prototype to achieve an output-to-input ratio of 2.1 and a net positive flow rate of 66 mL/min.
Continuous heat input inside the hot accumulator prevents cyclic performance decay over time and allows fluid-only actuation to reach an output-to-input ratio of 1.35.

experimental_setup: Two opposing wet SMA actuators coupled to two positive-displacement diaphragm pumping chambers through a pivoting lever with adjustable mechanical advantage
Hot and cold water accumulators providing pressurized flow (tested at 15 kPa) through supply tubing and actuators
Continuous electric immersion heating element placed inside the hot accumulator to maintain water temperature
Four solenoid valves arranged into an inlet routing manifold and an outlet separation manifold to cycle and recycle hot and cold fluids
Two external DC power supplies connected across the SMA wires to provide timed auxiliary Joule heating pulses
Testing conducted at an elevation of approximately 1400 m with local water boiling temperature around 88 deg C
future_work: Making the robotic pump system more compact in volume without impairing SMA contraction
Removing the need for auxiliary electrical inputs by using fluid-only heating and mechanically timed valve mechanisms
Characterizing and optimizing practical thermodynamic efficiency by minimizing thermal and mechanical losses
Powering continuous, silent operation using high-energy-density chemical energy sources instead of electrical heating
independent_variables: SMA actuator length (tested from 20 cm to 45 cm, notably 35-45 cm and 40 cm)
Mechanical advantage of the pumping lever (e.g., 0.84 and lower)
Fluid flow duration per cycle (varied between 1.0 s and 5.0 s)
Electrical Joule heating lead time relative to fluid flow shutoff (0 to 1.0 s)
Heat input status in the hot accumulator (continuous heat addition vs. no heat addition)
Accumulator operating pressure (tested at 15 kPa and lower pressures)
limitations_inferred: The system relies on external electrical power supplies to drive the four solenoid routing valves and provide Joule heating, preventing it from functioning as a fully untethered system in its current state.

Because water is utilized as the working fluid in an open cycle system, boiling temperature constraints vary with elevation and atmospheric pressure, making performance sensitive to ambient altitude unless pressurized closed loops are used.
Potential thermal degradation and progressive fluid mixing across the separation manifolds during prolonged operation were not evaluated over long-term cyclic testing.
Fatigue life, cycle degradation, and functional drift of the Nitinol wire under repeated rapid forced-convection and Joule heating cycles were not investigated.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The maximum theoretical efficiency of the system is only 3.4%, and the practical efficiency of the prototype is much lower due to environmental heat losses, fluid mixing, and parasitic mechanical losses.
The pump is relatively inefficient when compared to conventional electric motor-driven pumps.

Fluid-only actuation at the testing elevation (1400 m, boiling point ~88 deg C) could not exceed an output-to-input ratio of 1.0 without reducing accumulator pressure (which lengthened cycle times unfavorably) or adding electrical Joule heating.
Prolonged application of electric current through the SMA wire causes permanent deformation, restricting electrical heating duration to short pulses (1 s).
Decreasing mechanical advantage below 0.84 to increase displacement risks tensile stress exceeding the pulling strength of the SMA wire.
The current prototype is bulky and depends on auxiliary electrical inputs and solenoid manifolds.
main_results: Successfully designed, modeled, and implemented the first robotic pump capable of self-actuation via thermofluidic feedback with a net positive fluidic output.

Achieved a maximum experimental volumetric output-to-input ratio of 0.88 with fluid-only actuation under baseline conditions (15 kPa accumulator pressure) and up to 1.35 with continuous accumulator heat addition.

Achieved a maximum experimental volumetric output-to-input ratio of 2.1 using 40-cm actuators, 1.5-s flow duration, continuous accumulator heating, and 4.5-A auxiliary Joule heating (1.54 without continuous accumulator heating).
Generated a net positive fluidic output flow rate of 66 mL/min, which is two orders of magnitude greater than prior SMA micropumps.
Dynamic simulations matched experimental output-to-input ratios within 5% to 10% across varying actuator lengths and flow timings.
Demonstrated that continuous heat addition in the accumulator is critical for preventing output decay over successive pumping cycles.
modeling_methods: Energy bond graph modeling integrated with state-space representation coupling wet SMA actuators, mechanical lever kinematics, and pumping chambers
One-dimensional dynamic heat transfer equations modeling forced convection and conduction among fluid, SMA wire, compliant tube, and ambient air
Discretized multi-segment representation of the wet SMA actuators (20 segments per actuator)
Differential hysteresis model for martensite fraction using a cumulative normal distribution function modulated by wire temperature
Piecewise linear constitutive model capturing twinned martensite, detwinned martensite, and austenite elastic moduli and phase transformation stresses
Lumped-parameter fluid dynamic state equations for piston chamber pressures accounting for volumetric capacitance, fluidic resistance, and check valves
possible_gap_implications: Demonstrating an output-to-input ratio above 2.0 confirms that thermofluidic feedback is viable for driving macroscale soft robotic actuators, but eliminating electrical dependence via passive mechanical valving and chemical heating remains necessary to realize untethered operation.

While low thermodynamic efficiency remains an intrinsic challenge for thermal SMA actuation, coupling such pumps with high-energy-density chemical fuels could potentially offer system-level energy density advantages over battery-electric soft robotic pumps.
paper.research_objective: To design, optimize, model, and experimentally validate a biologically inspired wet SMA-actuated robotic pump that uses thermofluidic self-feedback to sustain its own actuation while delivering a net positive macroscale fluidic output to power external wet SMA robotic subsystems.
paper.research_problem: SMA actuators traditionally suffer from low bandwidth due to slow cooling and heating rates, and prior attempts to build self-sustaining SMA pumps failed to produce sufficient fluidic output to sustain their own actuation (output-to-input ratio <= 1.0), while existing microscale SMA pumps are limited to micro-liter flow rates incapable of driving macroscale robotic actuators.
paper.title: A Biologically Inspired Wet Shape Memory Alloy Actuated Robotic Pump
